item.title: Mova LiDAX Ultra 3000 AWD review: Built for tough lawns
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros Excellent traction on slopes and uneven ground Good obstacle detection and avoidance No boundary wire required Cons Automatic mapping struggled on a complicated lawn Expensive Large and heavy for smaller yards Our Verdict The Mova LiDAX Ultra 3000 AWD is a capable robot mower for challenging terrain, with excellent traction and dependable performance once its boundaries are established. Its unreliable automatic mapping, however, is a significant drawback at this price. Price When Reviewed This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Pricing Today Best Prices Today: Mova LiDAX Ultra 3000 AWD Retailer Price $2399 View Deal Home Depot $2399 View Deal $2399 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide The Mova LiDAX Ultra 3000 AWD is built for the kinds of lawns that can give robot mowers a lot of trouble: medium-to-large yards with slopes, uneven ground, and irregular shapes. I tested it on a roughly 7,600-square-foot lawn with all three, plus trees, a play structure, bare patches, mulch borders, and a raised strip of grass beside a fence, with a narrow gap below it. At $2,399—discounted from a $2,999 list price—the LiDAX is a premium mower aimed at homeowners whose terrain demands more than a basic model can deliver. Mova LiDAX Ultra 3000 AWD: Design and specs The LiDAX Ultra 3000 AWD is a hefty mower, measuring 29.1 × 20.9 × 12.6 inches and weighing 52 pounds. Its UltraDrive system uses four 116-watt hub motors to drive the wheels, while independent suspension and omni wheels help it stay stable on uneven ground and turn in tight spaces. Controls on top of the mower let you enter its anti-theft PIN and perform basic tasks without opening the app, including starting or stopping a mowing job and sending the mower back to its charging station. A large red stop button provides a quick way to halt the mower in an emergency. The Mova LiDAX Ultra 3000 AWD uses four driven wheels and a raised LiDAR sensor to navigate difficult terrain without a boundary wire. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry A raised 360-degree 3D LiDAR sensor on top of the mower scans its surroundings, while two forward-facing AI cameras identify lawn boundaries and potential obstacles. A physical bumper on the front of the mower provides another layer of detection when something makes contact with it. Together, these systems let the LiDAX navigate without a perimeter wire. Mova rates the mower for a single lawn up to 0.75 acre. It can store two maps, each covering up to 0.75 acre, and manage up to 150 mowing zones. Its 15.8-inch cutting deck can be adjusted through the app to cut grass from 1.2 to 3.9 inches high. The cutting disc shifts toward the side of the chassis near a raised boundary, which Mova says lets it trim within 1.2 inches of walls, fences, and similar edges. Mova also says the mower can climb an 80-percent grade and cross vertical obstacles up to 2.36 inches high. Its 7.5Ah battery is rated for 150 to 170 minutes of mowing and 0.2 to 0.25 acre of coverage per charge. Mova LiDAX Ultra 3000 AWD: Setup and mapping The mower comes with a charging station and power supply, ground anchors, cable pegs, replacement blades, and the hardware needed to install them. The charging station needs to be placed on level ground with a clear approach so the mower can enter and exit unobstructed. Once I found a suitable spot, I connected the power cable and secured the station and cable with the included anchors and pegs. A flip-up panel on the LiDAX Ultra 3000 AWD reveals its onboard display and controls for basic functions, including starting or stopping a mowing job and returning the mower to its charging station. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry Connecting the mower to the MovaHome app was even quicker. The app recognized the mower immediately and pairing it with my phone and connecting it to Wi-Fi took only a couple of minutes. The mower arrived locked, so I had to enter its PIN using the onboard controls before proceeding. The app then ran it through a short calibration routine. The app offers automatic and manual mapping. With AI mapping, the mower identifies the grass and traces the perimeter on its own. Manual mapping requires driving it around the boundary with the app’s virtual joystick. I started with AI mapping, but the lawn proved too complicated. Where the boundary was irregular or poorly defined, the mower sometimes left the lawn and became stuck. On one attempt, it drove into a broad mulch-covered area beside the play structure. On others, it fell over the raised edge near the fence. The MovaHome app provides quick access to mowing modes, manual control, cutting height, mowing direction, and other job settings. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry After several attempts, I gave up on AI mapping and drove the mower around the perimeter myself. That worked, but it erased much of the setup advantage automatic mapping was supposed to provide. The feature might fare better on a flatter lawn with sharper boundaries. On this property, it wasn’t dependable. Mova LiDAX Ultra 3000 AWD: Mowing performance Once the manual map was in place, the LiDAX behaved like a different mower. It traveled systematically up and down the lawn in parallel passes, while the app showed its live position, the area already cut, and its progress through the job. More important, it respected the boundary I had created. It never wandered onto the mulch or veered off the grass while mowing, even though those same areas had confused it during AI mapping. Its all-wheel drive provided plenty of traction to cross the lawn’s slopes, dips, and uneven patches without wheel-spinning or stalling. It also maneuvered cleanly around the trees, play structure, and other obstacles. Mova says the LiDAR and cameras can recognize more than 300 types of stationary and moving obstacles. The app can classify detected objects and assign a confidence rating; in one instance, it identified a person with 90-percent confidence. It also lets you report a mistaken identification and, if you enable the feature, capture photos of detected obstacles. The mower left open areas looking evenly trimmed. I didn’t find obvious missed strips or clumps of poorly cut grass, and it worked close enough around obstacles that little follow-up trimming was needed. Mova LiDAX Ultra 3000 AWD: App experience The MovaHome app puts the information you need during a mowing job on one screen. It shows the mower’s battery and connection status, live position, mapped area, completed area, and overall progress. Start, pause, end, and return-to-station controls are also easy to reach. During AI mapping, the MovaHome app alerted me when the LiDAX became stuck and needed assistance. Michael Ansaldo/Foundry A drop-down menu allows you to switch between all-area, edge, zone, spot, and manual mowing using the virtual joystick. You can choose standard or efficient mowing, adjust cutting height electronically, set the mowing direction, and enable automatic edge mowing. Settings can apply across the whole lawn or vary by zone, and recurring jobs can be scheduled for specific days and times. The app also supports rain protection, frost protection, do-not-disturb hours, recharge-and-resume operation, work logs, and maintenance tracking. Despite the number of options, it rarely feels crowded, and the main controls are easy to find. Should you buy the Mova LiDAX Ultra 3000 AWD? The LiDAX Ultra 3000 AWD didn’t deliver the automatic mapping experience Mova advertises, at least not on my complicated lawn. Driving the mower around the perimeter to map the boundary manually took more time and effort, but it also solved the mower’s navigation problems. Once the map was saved, the LiDAX stayed on the grass, handled slopes and uneven ground, and traveled along a narrow raised edge that had defeated a smaller robot mower. That makes it particularly appealing for medium-to-large lawns with difficult terrain, provided you’re willing to take over the mapping if the AI struggles. Buyers mainly attracted by the promise of effortless automatic setup should be more cautious. Its size and $2,399 price are also hard to justify for a small, uncomplicated yard.

item.title: Microsoft is killing its ‘Companion’ taskbar mini-apps in December
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Back in August 2025, Microsoft launched a new kind of software initiative called “Microsoft 365 Companions,” which were like mini-apps that lived within the taskbar and served a middle-of-the-road solution between simple notifications and complex Widgets. When they first launched, there were three Microsoft 365 Companions immediately available: People, which showed your favorite contacts and let you search your full contact list; Files, which could search, preview, and share cloud files without fully opening them; and Calendar, which let you join Teams calls without opening the full app. But now, just over a year since these Companions were first announced, Microsoft has decided to discontinue them. It’s unclear why they’re being discontinued—Microsoft offers no explanation. According to this Microsoft 365 support page , all three companion apps will be going into retirement starting on December 16th, 2026. You can keep using these until then, and once they’re removed, you won’t lose any data and no other existing Microsoft 365 features will be impacted. Since Microsoft 365 Companions are mostly managed by organization administrators, you may not have to do anything—they will be removed when the administrators trigger the removal. But if you aren’t part of an organization, you’ll have to remove them yourself. You can do this by navigating to Windows Settings → Apps → Installed apps. As far as what you can use in place of them once removed, Microsoft offers the following guidance: For calendar and people information, use Outlook and Teams. For files, use Windows Search Box, File Explorer, SharePoint, OneDrive, Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and more. You can also use Copilot, even when you only remember a few details about what you’re looking for.

item.title: Google Chrome is a privacy nightmare. Fix these settings
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Chrome is the most popular browser in the world by a country mile. With more than 77% of the browser market across all kinds of devices, it’s most people’s first choice—especially after a fresh Windows install . But Chrome isn’t some privacy-centric upstart that puts the user first. Just like Google’s “free” search engine, Chrome’s users are the product. The browser collects a lot of information about how, when, and where it’s used, and that can make some people uneasy. If you’re in the nothing-to-hide, nothing-to-fear camp, feel free to mosey along and enjoy your browsing experience with Chrome ( resource hog or not ). But if you’d rather limit how much data Chrome, and by extension, Google, has on you, there are steps you can take. We don’t know everything Chrome gathers; Google keeps those details deliberately vague. But thanks to court filings, independent studies, and forensic testing from privacy researchers, we do have a clear picture of some of the data Chrome collects behind the scenes. Here’s what the evidence shows, and what you can do about it. PROMOTION Ever wonder how scammers get your number? Data brokers collect and sell your personal info, including your phone number, to advertisers and fraudsters. PCWorld recommends using Incogni to automatically remove your data from these sites, helping to protect you from spam, scams, and identity theft. Don’t Miss Out Telemetry data: How you use the browser Disabling telemetry data in Chrome can help restore some privacy. Jon Martindale Just about every app collects data on how you use the app in question. It’s one of the best tools the developers have for figuring out what works and what doesn’t, and how they can improve the user experience based on the very real habits of its users. Chrome does much the same, but it’s certainly not something you have to be onboard with if you don’t want to. Chrome actually has a built-in tool for disabling at least a portion of its telemetry recording. In the Chrome browser, select the three-dot menu icon in the top-right, then Settings > You and Google and look for Help improve Chrome’s features and performance . Toggle it off. To further restrict how Google tracks you across sites and services, you can logout of the browser and change Chrome’s sign-in habits. Navigate to Settings > You and Google and consider some of the available options. Select the Sign out of Chrome button to log out. You can also use the drop-down menu on the right to decide what happens when you sign in to other Google services. You don’t have to sign in to Chrome just to take advantage of your YouTube Premium account . Your browsing history: The websites you visit Reduce unwanted tracking by changing Chrome’s settings on web searches. Jon Martindale Unsurprisingly, Google’s Chrome web browser knows the websites you visit while using it. It’s been caught out collecting even in incognito mode in the past and had to settle a lawsuit just a few years ago, deleting enormous reams of data on user browser activity that it collected, even when it wasn’t supposed to. Although we probably can’t trust Google to entirely disregard what you’re looking at in Chrome, you can at least tell it not to track some of it. Using incognito mode is a good start, but you can also adjust Chrome’s settings to reduce the chance it’s tracking which websites you visit. Navigate to Settings > You and Google and next to Make searches and browsing better make sure to toggle that option to Off . For good measure, also turn off Enhanced spell check , as that sends what you’re typing to Google. It’ll stop the spellchecker working, but it’s a small price to pay for enhancing your privacy (at least a little). You might also want to navigate to Settings > You and Google > Sync and Google services , and toggle off Improve search suggestions so that you only send your searches to whatever search engine you’re using, not also to your default one (which is probably Google). If you don’t mind reducing your security a little, you can also navigate to Settings > Privacy and security > Security and make sure that under Safe browser , you select No protection . Any other option sends at least a portion of the URL you’re visiting and the page content to Google to check if it’s safe or not. Also toggle off Help improve security on the web for everyone for similar reasons. Alternatively, if you want to improve your protection, the AI enhanced safe browsing feature is interesting . Your purchasing habits and advert effectiveness Reducing the amount of personalized ads through Chrome can help reduce another layer of data collection. Jon Martindale Google makes the majority of its money from advert sales, which is why it wants to collect so much data on its users in the first place: to better target ads at them. Although you can’t stop Google sharing some information with advertisers, you can reduce the amount the adverts that do reach you that are personalized. Select the three-dot menu icon and navigate to Settings > Privacy and security . Select Ads privacy followed by each of the tree options in turn: Ad topics , Site-suggested ads , and Ads measurement . Toggle all of them to off to restrict the data Chrome shares with advertisers. Alternatively, you can sack off all the adverts altogether by using an adblocker. Popular options include Ublock Origin and Ghostery and they’re simple to install – they’re some of my favorite Chrome extensions , in fact. You may need to chop and change which one you use on occasion, though, as Google and Chrome updates regularly break certain functions of one blocker or another. It’s an ongoing cat and mouse game. Extra tips worth considering Alongside advertisers, Chrome also helps others collect data on you and your browsing habits too. Using anti-tracker and advert blocking extensions and apps is the best way to block them out, but you can also use Chrome to make it more difficult for them as well. Navigate to Settings > Privacy and security > Third Party Cookies . Toggle on the Block third-party cookies off to cut down on what other sites and services can track about you, though certain site features may not work correctly. Navigate to Settings > Privacy and security > Third Party Cookies and toggle Send a ‘Do not Track’ request with your browsing traffic , to On . There’s no guarantee a site will listen to it, but if they do, it’s there at least. Settings > Privacy and security > Delete browsing data . You can do this manually to remove any browsing data Chrome has collected on you, but you can also have it do it automatically after you close the browser, or on a trigger of your setting. It won’t stop Chrome collecting any data, but it will make sure there’s no record of it on your local machine. Using another browser The ultimate way to stop Google collecting so much data about you via Chrome, is to simply not use Chrome. I know that’s a tricky proposition when it’s so often the default browser option and much of the internet is built with Chrome in mind. However, that’s not as strictly true as it might seem and you don’t even need to ditch the style of browser you’ve grown used to in moving over. Chrome is based on the Chromium open source project but it’s not the only one. It’s the underlying core of Opera , Microsoft’s Edge , Vivaldi , and the Brave Browser . Any of them will feel quite similar to Chrome, even if they don’t work in quite the same way. There’s also the venerable Firefox , which privacy proponents tend to be quite fond of. There’s also Colibri for a very minimalist browser experience, or Maxthon, which makes bold claims about its lack of user tracking. Give one of them a try. You might find you like it.

item.title: These hidden Windows 11 tools can save your PC — and your workday
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Ideally, your PC will work smoothly day in and day out. But when something goes wrong, you should have a game plan for solving your problems — and there’s even some new, updated features within Windows for doing so. I happened to live in London during the run of The IT Crowd , the Channel 4 production that helped launch the careers of Richard Ayoade and Chris O’Dowd. The two characters manned the help desk, and the show’s catchphrase was a simple one: “Have you tried turning it off and on again?” A simple reboot can often solve most of your computer problems…and it allowed the characters on the show to go back to doing nothing. If that doesn’t work, however, it’s time to try a few other strategies. Windows 11 now offers a surprising array of repair, recovery, and troubleshooting options to keep your PC working hard for you. Welcome to PCWorld’s newsletter, Smart Mode! The focus of this newsletter is productivity: from software to hardware to peripherals, all with the idea to get what you need to get done, efficiently. I’m your host, Mark Hachman, covering the productivity tips, tools, and trends that you need to know about, both from within PCWorld and beyond. If you want the latest issue in your inbox each week, just sign up right here . Troubleshooters: tried and true I’d swear that Microsoft said that it was getting rid of its Windows 11 PC troubleshooters, but they’re still the first place I go if I have a problem with my PC. The controls can be found within the System > Troubleshoot menu within the Windows 11 Settings. Supposedly, they’re somewhat autonomous, as my PC directs Windows to ask me before running them. (To my knowledge, it never has.) I immediately jump down to System > Troubleshoot > Other troubleshooters — which is what you want, and it feels a little odd that Microsoft is hiding them here. If my laptop is having issues connecting to the Internet, I run the “Network and Internet” troubleshooter. Occasionally I’ll have reason to run the “Printer” troubleshooter, and I’ve run the ‘Windows Update” troubleshooter once before, too. Mark Hachman / Foundry Each troubleshooter simply launches its own procedure to solve the problem, and usually does. (At one time, this is what I thought Copilot running locally on your PC might do, and I wonder if Microsoft could one day dedicate its own troubleshooting AI agents within Windows to solving these problems.) If your PC somehow fails to boot, Microsoft also has what it calls Quick Machine Recovery , which is basically an automatic cloud-based troubleshooter. It should run automatically and is on by default inside the Settings menu ( System > Recovery > Quick machine recovery ), too. But wait — Microsoft has other troubleshooting solutions that you might not know about! Restore points are now more powerful You may know about Windows restore points , which saves a snapshot of your system at a given point in time. These have existed for years — far enough back that they’re managed by the Control Panel. The idea is that if something on your PC goes wrong, you can “time travel” back to when it worked correctly. Mark Hachman / Foundry What’s the weakness of a restore point? It saves a snapshot of just the operating system, and nothing else. A traditional restore point is a hedge against a Windows update that you might be nervous about, as it’s a way to roll back to an earlier, “safer” release. Microsoft now has something new: a “point in time restore” feature that goes beyond what the “system restore” offers: it backs up the OS, apps, settings, and local files (though no user data is scoped out of the restore point, Microsoft says.) It’s on by default, saving every 24 hours and automatically deleting them after 72 hours. The problem? If a.) your PC created a restore point, then b.) you created a file, and then c.) you roll back to the restore point, your new file disappears. If you have to go deeper, the Deployment Image Servicing and Management (DISM) tool within the Command Line Interface is a sign that something is more seriously wrong with your PC. You may need to repair a Windows image using the tool, or use the related SFC command (sfc /scannow) to scan for corrupted files. DISM can get messy very quickly, which is why there have been some attempts to develop GUI-based interfaces. (Our command-line tools article has more on this.) Alternatively, some people swear by Microsoft’s Sysinternals as a collection of troubleshooting tools , though I feel like the average user will think the collection is too nerdy for what they want to do. The final step: reset your PC This has traditionally been the last and final step towards fixing a borked PC: throwing up your hands and reinstalling Windows . But even then, you have multiple options! This was traditionally the way to reset your PC : keep your personal files (but remove apps and settings) or remove everything and start over. Since then, you’ve had even more options: reload Windows from a stored copy on your hard drive or SSD, or re-download it from the cloud . But Microsoft has even more options than what my colleagues have written about. The first, also available via the Windows settings ( System > Recovery) is called “Fix problems without resetting your PC,” preserving all of your apps, files and settings. The idea is that this solution will “fix system component corruption” by reinstalling the current version of Windows. Mark Hachman / Foundry The oddest addition to this list isn’t within the Windows Settings menu at all. The Windows Security app now includes what Microsoft calls “Fresh start.” “Start fresh with a clean and up-to-date installation of Windows” the app says. “This will keep your personal files and some Windows settings, and remove some of your apps. In some cases, this may improve your device’s startup and shutdown experience, memory usage, Store apps performance, browsing experience and battery life.” (Emphasis mine.) The problem is that “Fresh start” doesn’t have an action associated with it, such as a button you can press. It’s essentially a suggestion to reset your PC, with a confusing statement that some of your settings will be preserved. I have no idea why it’s there. Thankfully, with all of the other troubleshooting and recovery options available to you, you shouldn’t need it! Productivity in the news: I can’t wait to get my hands on a Googlebook, though for now I’ll have to wait. My colleague Michael Crider notes how closely Googlebooks integrate with Android , though I’ve noted how well Samsung phones and PCs do the same . Ben Patterson is a bit surprised that they’re not just Geminibooks . And, of course, there are five to choose from . What else? It’s a $2,499 Mac workstation . Is it productive? Yeah, should be. Everyone loves free utilities. Sam Singleton has a new one: a universal file converter . How to use color coding to highlight informative emails in Outlook. Asus ProArt KD300 keyboard review : why is this being marketed at professionals? Alex Wawro pines for a tiling window manager. He found one in *sigh* Linux. Productivity on camera: The Windows Clock app includes Focus Mode…which does just that. Here’s how it works . Productivity tip of the week: Work-life boundaries. This was actually a topic that came up while we were planning out my son’s trip to college (UC Santa Cruz, home of the Fighting Banana Slugs). I did actually send my son to school with these tech essentials for his dorm room that I decided upon a month or so ago. When I was at school, though, I lived in the architecture building next door to my dorm, studying and working on their massive Surface Studio-sized displays for writing papers. My father had his own little niche in an empty classroom. My wife used the library. The point is that none of us lived and studied/worked in the same space, which did make me wonder if I had wasted my money. That’s why an office is a good idea — and why, post-pandemic, much of the world woke up to the fact that we didn’t need to actually leave the house to find one. Still, a dedicated work space is a good idea, as it trains your mind to move into productivity mode when your body enters it. Likewise, you also need a space for you , where you can recharge. Thanks for reading! Thanks for tuning in to this edition of Smart Mode, PCWorld’s newsletter devoted to helping you make the most of your life, smartly. Sign up and have it sent to your inbox every Thursday!

Running out of disk space on Windows 10/11 can trigger low disk space warnings and interfere with updates. In many cases, you can reclaim space without buying a larger drive or paid software. This guide covers five free ways to free up disk space, from Windows cleanup tools to partition management. If deleting files isn’t enough, you’ll also learn how to merge partitions to fix a full C drive. Quick Summary: How to Free Up Disk Space? [Windows Built-in Tool] 5 Free Ways to Free Up Disk Space on Windows If you need to free up space on Windows 10/11 without spending money, start with these five methods. 1. Use Storage Sense to Clean Up Temporary Files Storage Sense automatically removes temporary files and other items you no longer need, helping free up disk space. Go to Settings > System > Storage > Storage Sense and turn it on. You can also select Run Storage Sense now to start a cleanup manually. Based on your settings, Storage Sense can also manage items such as Recycle Bin contents, Downloads, and cloud storage. Best for: Temporary files and routine cleanup. 2. Extend C Drive with Unallocated Space Not every low disk space issue is caused by too many files. If your C drive is nearly full but another partition has plenty of unused space, you can combine them using the partition merge feature. For example: Partition Total Space Used Space C: 120 GB 112 GB D: 500 GB 200 GB In this case, deleting a few more temporary files may only be a short-term fix. Right-click the C: drive and select Merge . Select the target partition (such as D:) whose space you want to combine into the C: drive, then click OK . Click Execute Task , then Apply to confirm the changes. EaseUS Note: The exact steps may vary depending on your partition layout and whether the partitions are adjacent. Back up important files and double-check the selected partitions before you proceed. Best for: A full C drive when another partition has enough unused space. FREE DOWNLOAD 3. Use Disk Cleanup to Free Up Space Search for Disk Cleanup in the Windows Start menu, select the drive you want to clean, and review the file categories to completely delete the Windows.old folder on Windows 10 to remove outdated OS backups. You can typically remove standard items such as: Temporary files Thumbnails Downloaded Program Files Delivery Optimization Files Recycle Bin Note: Be careful when removing Previous Windows installation(s) . Deleting these files permanently removes the Windows.old folder and prevents you from rolling back to your previous version of Windows. Best for: Removing temporary and system files identified by Windows as safe to delete. 4. Delete or Move Large Personal Files Large videos, photos, downloads, installers, and other personal files can quickly consume C drive space. Instead of deleting files you still need, move them to another drive, external storage, or cloud storage. Open File Explorer > This PC , check folders such as Downloads, Videos, Pictures, and Documents , and sort files by Size to find the largest ones first. If you are not sure what is taking up the most space, a free disk space analyzer such as EaseUS Partition Master can help you visualize which files and folders use the most storage. Before deleting anything, make sure you no longer need the files or have a backup. Best for: Finding large personal files and moving them off a crowded C drive. 5. Uninstall Apps You No Longer Use Unused apps and games can take up significant disk space. Windows includes a built-in uninstall tool, so you do not need additional software for basic app removal. Press Windows + I to open Settings , then go to Apps . Windows 10 users : Select Apps & features . Windows 11 users : Select Installed apps . Browse through the list or sort apps by Size to locate heavy programs and games. Click the app menu (or the three dots) and select Uninstall , then follow the on-screen prompts. Focus on large programs and games you no longer use, but avoid removing apps or system components if you are unsure what they do. Best for: Freeing up space used by large, unused apps and games. And then we’ve got the Asus ROG Zephyrus Duo , which is the unicorn of the gaming laptop world. It’s got two 16-inch OLED 2880×1800 displays that you can position either horizontally or vertically. How we test gaming laptops The PCWorld team puts each and every Windows laptop through a series of benchmarks that test GPU and CPU performance, battery life, and so on. The idea is to push the laptop to its limits and then compare it against others we’ve tested. Chromebooks, on the other hand, undergo a series of web-based tests. For a much deeper look at our review methodology, check out how PCWorld tests laptops . Who curated this article? Hi, I’m Ashley Biancuzzo , and I oversee all laptop and Chromebook coverage at PCWorld. While you’ll see me review Chromebooks on occasion, I’m also really into the broader world of consumer tech. I spend a lot of time writing and thinking about where laptops are headed, from AI and sustainable designs to long-term trends. When I’m not deep in the world of tech, you’ll probably find me gaming, getting lost in a good book, or chilling with my rescue greyhound, Allen. How to choose the best gaming laptop To find the best gaming laptop for your needs, pay close attention to the following features. What’s the best screen for a gaming laptop? When you buy a gaming laptop, one of the most important decisions you’ll need to make regards the screen. After all, what you get on day one is what you’re stuck with until you junk the device. You could run an external monitor, but then what’s the point of a laptop? Look for an IPS or OLED display, though gaming laptops under $1,000 sometimes feature a TN panel. You can get by with a 60Hz display if you mostly play single-player games, but thankfully, most gaming laptops these days opt for faster 120Hz+ panels instead. What’s the best screen size for a gaming laptop? The size of the screen dictates the size of the laptop itself, and thus weight. Think long and hard about whether you’re willing to take the weight penalty in exchange for the screen real estate. What’s the best screen resolution for a gaming laptop? The buzzword today is “4K.” That high resolution delivers sharper photo viewing and more space for video editing, but that doesn’t mean it’s for everyone. Anything not using the panel’s native resolution of 3840×2180, such as games running at lower-than-4K resolution, won’t look quite as sharp unless you exponentially increase the graphics power of the laptop. If you’re running at 1920×1080 resolution because your GPU can’t hit 60fps at 4K, that feature is moot. For many gamers, 1920×1080 (1080p) or 2560×1440 (1440p) is more optimal. IPS vs. TN vs. OLED: What’s the difference? The panel technology is a key feature. IPS (in-plane switching) generally produces much greater color accuracy and superior off-axis viewing, but tends to lag in response times, which can lead to blurring. TN (twisted nematic) panels can offer far higher refresh rates and usually better response times than IPS, but can look washed out or just blah. A middle-ground technology that’s appearing more often is VA (vertical alignment). VA is sometimes alternately referred to as “wide viewing angle” technology. (Many assume this spec to be IPS, but it’s not). In our experience, we’ve found VA panels to run the gamut from being worthy competitors to IPS to being worse than the better TN panels. The wildcard in all this is OLED. Unlike IPS, TN, and VA, OLED panels don’t rely on edge- or backlighting where “black” is produced by a shutter-like mechanism that blocks light from coming through. Instead, each pixel generates its own light. To produce black, it just switches off the light. This amounts to truly stunning contrast ratios and vibrant colors. OLEDs also boast fantastic response times. The negatives include smaller screen sizes (we haven’t seen anything larger than 15.6 inches yet), higher cost, and lack of support for variable refresh rate. OLED panels can also use more power than conventional methods if the image is on a white background. Should a gaming laptop have G-Sync or FreeSync support? Okay, we called this section G-Sync and FreeSync, but the reality is, when it comes to beefy gaming laptops, it’s a GeForce GPU world. And that means it’s a G-Sync world. In a nutshell, Nvidia and AMD’s respective variable-refresh-rate technologies help synchronize the monitor and the GPU to greatly reduce screen tearing. Variable refresh rates can make gaming at 40fps far smoother to your eyes than a screen without it. The first variable-refresh-rate panels for laptops maxed out at 75Hz, only marginally better than the standard 60Hz. More recently, we’ve begun to see laptop panels that can push 120Hz, 144Hz, and even 240Hz. This generally means smoother and sharper gaming to your eyes. It even helps smooth out everyday tasks such as scrolling a browser page or Word document. One last very important note: G-Sync screens have to be connected directly to the laptop’s discrete GPU, which means a large hit on battery life. In most laptops without G-Sync, the Intel integrated graphics is connected directly to the screen, so the GPU can be turned off when not being used. So while G-Sync is beautiful to behold, the cost in battery life is huge. What should you look for in a gaming laptop keyboard and trackpad? A new trend in gaming laptops is the offset trackpad, which is more conducive to gaming than a dead-center trackpad. The concept is sound, but anyone who actually cares about PC gaming will just plug in a mouse. The worst thing about that offset trackpad is when you try to use it for non-gaming purposes. As far as keyboards go, the most important gaming feature is n-key rollover. This means the keyboard physically scans each key separately. If you wanted to, you could press 20 keys simultaneously and they’d all register, as each is independently wired. That probably sounds excessive, but keyboards that lack this feature can suffer missed keystrokes, which both ruins gameplay and hurts in everyday tasks. Other keyboard considerations include LED backlighting (which adds ambiance but does nothing for gameplay) and mechanical keys vs. membrane. Mechanical keys are excellent, but are available on only a handful of laptops that usually weigh a ton. We have seen a few designs with low-profile mechanical keyboards, but even we admit they can be an acquired taste. What kind of storage is best for a gaming laptop? Having your games load from an SSD instead of a hard drive significantly cuts down on load times. But beyond that, we haven’t found it to matter that much whether it’s a super-fast NVMe PCIe drive or a slower SATA SSD. What does matter more today is the size of the SSD rather than the interface it uses. With games now topping 50GB and some touching 100GBs, a once-spacious 256GB SSD will feel too small with just four games installed. So when spec’ing out that gaming laptop, be mindful of just how much total storage you have. If you go for a laptop with a small SSD and large hard drive combo, expect to install your games to the hard drive. If the laptop will have an SSD only, choose an absolute minimum of 512GB, with 1TB preferred. How much RAM do you need in a gaming laptop? When laptop makers spec out gaming laptops, one of the levers they use to try to convince you to buy their product is upping the amount of RAM. It’s not hard to find gaming laptops with “upgraded” configurations that go from 16GB of RAM to 32GB. While having an adequate amount of RAM is important for gaming, today’s games typically top out at 16GB of RAM, and sometimes can run fine with just 8GB of RAM. Most people should invest in a gaming laptop with 16GB of memory if possible, and it makes sense to opt for 32GB if you plan on holding onto your gaming laptop for a long time. Modern games are only getting more memory-hungry. Should a gaming laptop have dual-channel or single-channel RAM? Besides the amount of memory, a couple of other important, but not critical, questions to ask is what clock speed and what mode. Modern CPUs let you run RAM in sets to increase the memory bandwidth. More memory bandwidth immediately helps laptops that are running integrated graphics, but the conventional wisdom has long been that discrete GPUs in laptops don’t benefit as much because they have their own dedicated, much faster GDDR5 RAM to use. That’s typically the case, but the performance of today’s GPUs and CPUs can make this conventional wisdom wrong. Gaming performance is often about a balance between the CPU and the GPU, and how graphically intensive a game is. With games that are graphically intensive, the GPU is the primary bottleneck on performance. Play a game that isn’t graphically intense, though, and the CPU can rapidly become the bottleneck on performance. With the power of today’s GPUs, a lot of games, especially at a sedate resolution of 1920×1080, have shifted more performance to the CPU. The reason we’re talking about this now is if you rob the CPU of memory bandwidth, even a decently fast one, you can take a sizable hit in gaming performance. The basic lesson is you should opt for dual-channel memory bandwidth configurations when possible. On a laptop spec sheet, you typically would see this expressed as “dual-channel” or “2 x 8” to indicate that two 8GB memory modules were used in a laptop. Some laptop makers will express memory in clock speed, so you’ll see “DDR4/2,133 or DDR4/2,400.” While a higher memory clock does increase memory bandwidth, the impact isn’t quite as great as going from dual-channel to single-channel mode. How many CPU cores do you really need in a gaming laptop? For most people on a budget, a 4-core CPU with Hyper-Threading will function just fine in most games, especially when combined with a lower-cost and lower performance GPU. Still, if you have the extra cash, a 6-core CPU with Hyper-Threading is likely the sweet spot for today and tomorrow. If you plan to stream your gaming live or edit it, investing in a 6-core is recommended. Intel and AMD’s top-end 8-plus-core CPUs will deliver the greatest benefit to those who might do other graphics-intensive tasks, such as 3D animation or video editing. If you also plan to record and stream video, the 8-core will offer a performance benefit there, too. If you’re thinking, great, let me buy a 4-core Core i5 or Ryzen 5 CPU with a luxury laptop to save money, you usually can’t, because PC makers typically only offer budget CPUs with other budget parts. Why? Well, most budget shoppers can’t afford any luxury items, and most PC makers like to add in the extras to increase the profit. What GPU is best for a gaming laptop? The single most important piece of hardware in a gaming laptop is undoubtedly the GPU. For AMD fans, the situation is as sad as it is in CPUs: It’s an Nvidia GeForce world. As with CPUs though, the good news is that the dominating products are top-notch. The hardest part will be deciding just how much GPU you need. Our general guidance is to buy as fast a GPU as you can afford and are willing to heft. Generally, the faster the GPU (or GPUs), the larger and heavier the laptop. If you’re talking about playing on a higher-resolution panel of 2560×1440 at high-refresh rates, then keep increasing the amount of money spent on the GPU. What kind of battery life should a gaming laptop have? The last topic we’ll cover is battery life. The best way to understand battery life on a gaming laptop is to accept that it’ll be horrible for all things gaming. The minute you crank up a GPU on a gaming laptop to play a game, you’re basically limiting yourself to an hour or an hour and a half of battery runtime. Period. And in some cases, far less than that. The only reason to consider battery life on a gaming laptop is if you want to use your laptop unplugged for non-gaming purposes. In that respect, you’ll find a lot of variance, with some offering decent battery life, albeit with a trade-off in gaming performance. FAQ 1. What is the best gaming laptop? The Alienware 16X Aurora is PCWorld’s top gaming laptop, delivering high-end performance without the ridiculously high price tag. 2. What is the best cheap gaming laptop? The Acer Nitro V 16 AI is PCWorld’s top budget gaming laptop. It offers good gaming performance and a spacious 16-inch, 1200p display for a low price. 3. When is the best time to buy a gaming laptop? The best time to pick up a gaming laptop is during Black Friday, Cyber Monday, or back-to-school season. Those deals will save you a lot of cash. 4. Should you get a gaming laptop or a PC? It really depends on your lifestyle. If you’re someone that’s always on-the-go, a gaming laptop is a good fit. But if you’re okay with staying in one spot and want more power or upgrade options, a PC is a better choice. 5. What’s the difference between a gaming laptop and a regular laptop? A gaming laptop is made for handling games, so it has beefed-up graphics and better cooling. A regular laptop, on the other hand, is designed for everyday stuff like browsing or working on documents and operating unplugged for extended periods of time. item.title: Windows 10 is more stable than Windows 11 in 2026, data shows
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Time and again, Microsoft has to issue fixes for Windows 11 because its monthly updates cause unexpected damage. But just how prone to errors is Windows 11 really, given the number of updates that constantly cause new problems? And how robust is Windows 10 in comparison? According to Windows Latest , which analyzed all the Windows updates released since January 2026, the results are unsurprising: Windows 10 is significantly more stable and reliable than Windows 11. Most recently, the Windows 11 September update broke USB audio and broke the File History feature , but it’s been a monthly pattern. August broke printers and PDFs , July broke certain Dell PCs , June broke startup and BitLocker recovery , all the way back to January. Of the nine months that have passed this year, Windows Latest found that eight of them involved at least one major issue or regression. Windows 10 hasn’t been flawless this year. For example, a June update caused a BitLocker user lockout problem , echoing a similar issue that flared up back in November 2025 . But on the whole, it’s been noticeably more stable, with fewer system crashes and catastrophes. One big reason for Windows 10’s greater stability is that it no longer receives new features. Ever since support ended in October 2025, Microsoft has only been pushing out security updates for Windows 10, and only for users who enrolled in the Extended Security Updates (ESU) program. With fewer sweeping changes, it’s less likely to break. So anyone who’s satisfied with Windows 10’s feature set, has no interest in Copilot AI, and prioritizes stability over fancy new features and experiments is clearly better off with Windows 10. Meanwhile, if you’re on Windows 11 and you’re experiencing system instability or other unexpected issues after installing an update, it’s usually best to roll back the update and wait for future fixes. Windows 11 also has a feature called Known Issue Rollback (KIR) that can revert buggy non-security features without uninstalling the whole update.

item.title: Microsoft is quietly killing its Copilot+ PC brand
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
When AI PCs first hit the market back in early 2024, Microsoft led the initiative with its hyped-up Copilot+ PC branding . The “Copilot+ PC” label was reserved for Windows machines that met minimum specs for running local AI features: an NPU with 40+ TOPS, at least 16GB of RAM, and at least 256GB of SSD storage, plus Windows 11 24H2 or later. But it seems the end is nigh for the whole Copilot+ PC movement. Windows Central reports that Microsoft’s newest 12-inch Surface Pro and 13-inch Surface Laptop, which were recently showcased at the Snapdragon Summit, both meet the hardware requirements for the Copilot+ PC badge… yet neither of them flaunts it. Jaime Marrero Microsoft’s Surface chief, Brett Ostrom, says that the two devices will not be referred to as Copilot+ devices, which would be a strange move if Microsoft intended to keep pushing the label. Meanwhile, Qualcomm’s SVP of compute and gaming, Kedar Kondap, reportedly told Windows Central that the Copilot+ PC badge is unlikely to be used in the future. The writing has been on the wall for a while now. Windows 11’s Copilot+ AI features were never well-received, feeling like early tech demos when they first launched and newer advancements failing to catch on. A year after debut, we explored all the ways Copilot+ PCs still needed to improve if the movement was going to succeed. That didn’t quite happen. Late last year, Microsoft was seemingly pushing all Windows 11 PCs to become AI PCs regardless of whether or not they qualify as Copilot+ PCs. Then earlier this year, Microsoft exercised deep reflection and came to the conclusion that maybe the right move is to pull back on its AI ambitions in Windows 11 and scale back on AI integration . To add insult to injury, reports suggest that no one is using Microsoft’s Copilot AI . Put it all together and it almost seems inevitable that Copilot+ would be sunset, if not this year then next. Note, however, that Ostrum didn’t say Microsoft is abandoning AI altogether: “[The new Surface Pro and Laptop] are not called Copilot+ PCs, [but] they do meet all the requirements of our previous bar for what Copilot+ devices are. We still lean into the narrative around AI on the edge and being able to have a hybrid solution out there.”

item.title: Want more PC storage space? This free duplicate-file finder is the key
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Our mobile phone cameras are taking increasingly better photos and videos, and this isn’t all good news. One of the consequences is that the files themselves are taking up more and more space, and this can become a problem for anyone who saves them on their computer. This is because computer storage capacity hasn’t grown at the same rate. On the contrary, many computers are now sold with fairly small hard drives, which means they quickly fill up. A simple way to save space is to delete all unnecessary duplicate files. Whether they’re photos, videos, or something else, it’s easy to end up saving the same large file in several different places, and this sometimes happens automatically if you’ve enabled various types of backup and synchronization. Finding duplicates is a tedious chore for a human, but much simple for a computer. A handy tool that does the job is called CCleaner . What is CCleaner? CCleaner is a popular computer cleaning program. It has been around for more than 20 years and has millions of users worldwide. The program can clean and optimize your computer in various ways, but the feature for finding duplicate files is one of the most useful. CCleaner is what’s known as a “freemium” program, which means the basic version is free, but there’s a paid version for those who want more features. It’s called CCleaner Professional and costs around $30 a year. The free version is sufficient for simply searching for duplicates, but it’s important to be aware that the manufacturer is quite aggressive in its marketing. The program displays warnings such as “You have an urgent performance problem,” but this is mainly a way of promoting the company’s paid service. As a general rule, you can ignore the warnings and instead focus on removing the duplicates. Here’s how to do it. 1. Install Foundry You can download CCleaner via the Microsoft Store . Using the search field on your PC, type CCleaner , click ‘Install’ and accept the warning. If you prefer a standard installer, go to www.ccleaner.com and select ‘Free Download .’ 2. Upgrade Foundry If you have an older version, you may need to upgrade to the latest version, called CCleaner 7.x, yourself. Depending on which version you have, you can do this via ‘ Check for updates ’ in the bottom right-hand corner. You can also do this via ‘Settings ’ > ‘Updates .’ 3. Start Foundry To start, open CCleaner, click ‘Duplicate Finder’ in the left-hand menu and select ‘Start Now .’ You can scan your entire computer by clicking ‘Drives’ and selecting a drive. You can also go to ‘Select specific folders,’ then ‘Browse’ to, for example, scan only your Documents folder. 4. Delete all duplicates Foundry Start the scan by clicking ‘Scan .’ Once it’s finished, all duplicates will be displayed in a list organized by file type. To remove all duplicates, click ‘Bulk Selection’ and choose ‘Keep the oldest files’ or ‘Keep the newest files .’ 5. Or just a few Foundry Deleting everything can be risky, so you can instead select ‘Deselect All’ and manually select the files you want to delete. When you’re done, in all cases click ‘Move to Bin’ (or ‘Delete’ if you don’t want to be able to recover the file). 6. View file Foundry You can find out more about a file by tapping the three dots on the right and selecting ‘View information .’ Use the link under ‘Location’ to open the folder where the file is stored. You can also delete the file by selecting ‘Move to Bin’ or ‘Delete’ (as in step 5). 7. Get more power Foundry The Duplicate Finder feature in CCleaner is simple and stripped-back. If you need a more powerful tool, Alldup is a popular free alternative. It has many advanced features for searching through large numbers of files, and offers greater scope for customizing it to your requirements. However, its interface may seem off-putting to inexperienced users. To install it, go to www.alldup.de/en and select ‘ Download ’ from the top menu. Click on ‘Alldup (Freeware)’ to open the download page. Click on the top ‘Download’ button and choose to save the file to a suitable location on your hard drive. Double-clicking the file will launch a self-explanatory installation program.

item.title: Is Windows 11 good enough yet?
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Windows 11 will be five years old on October 5th. Is it good enough yet to merit upgrading from Windows 10? The question is moot for me, since I reviewed Windows 11 back when it launched in 2021 and have been using it ever since. But for anyone still on the fence, it’s a question you should be asking yourself because you have the option of enrolling in the Windows 10 Extended Support Program to keep your classic OS updated with critical security patches through October 2027 . It’s also a question one viewer put to the hosts during the Q&A portion of this week’s The Full Nerd show, and it got me thinking: am I willing to change my tune on Windows 11 after watching it evolve for half a decade? I think I might be. I made peace with using Windows 11 as my daily driver years ago, but the ever-present ads for Microsoft products, disappointing optimization and AI nonsense turned my stomach. However, some recent projects we’ve been working on here at PCWorld made me realize it might be time for a second opinion. Welcome to The Full Nerd newsletter—your weekly dose of hardware talk from the enthusiasts at PCWorld. Missed the surprising topics on our YouTube show or the latest news from across the web? You’re in the right place. Want this newsletter to come directly to your inbox? Sign up on our website ! For example, I’ve been testing out the new Dell XPS 13 so we can shoot a video about it and I’ve been pleasantly surprised at how snappy and normal it feels to use despite only sporting 8GB of RAM. I recall that Windows 11 was quite a resource hog back when I reviewed it years ago on PCs with 16-32GB of RAM, so I expected the anemic XPS 13 would chug like a frat boy when I started multitasking. Instead, I’ve found it feels as snappy to navigate as my 32GB-equipped desktop PC, even when I have Chrome open with 20+ tabs while I’m streaming music and writing up something in Word. Sure, the laptop can’t hold a candle to my desktop when it comes to demanding tasks like gaming, video editing and the like, but for basic browsing and productivity work? I’d never have known this little XPS 13 was packing a paltry 8GB under the hood. Foundry / Ashley Biancuzzo At least, not until I opened the Task Manager and saw the memory usage at 6GB minimum even if nothing is open. Because while Windows 11 feels smooth and responsive on this 8GB laptop it still eats up a ton of resources, even while idling. Once I started launching apps and opening tabs that number climbed steadily, but in my limited testing I’ve yet to redline it or cause the system to stutter using just productivity apps. That got me thinking that maybe, just maybe, all the wailing and complaining writers like myself have done over the years has actually led the likes of Google and Microsoft to put in serious work optimizing their software for PC . Another project I’ve been working in is a video about Windows 11, and for one aspect of it I actually did a fresh install on a new machine and went looking for as many examples of annoying ads as I could find. I’m talking pop-up ads for OneDrive, intrusive reminders to put personal information into Windows, even that nagging pop-up to choose Bing instead when you go to download Chrome. I really wanted to snag evidence of as many annoying Windows 11 ads as I could find, but to my surprise it was a real struggle. That’s not to say there are no longer annoying ads for Microsoft products and services in Windows 11, just that they’re far less common and intrusive nowadays than I remember. That seems like a good thing, and while there are still things I don’t like about Microsoft’s latest operating system I have to grudgingly admit it’s gotten better with age. That’s faint praise, I know, but I’m not sure I could say the same about myself so I suppose I should cut Windows 11 some slack. Now if only Microsoft would sell a Pro edition for enthusiasts, like The Full Nerd team suggests! In this week’s episode of The Full Nerd On this week’s episode of The Full Nerd regular cohosts Alaina Yee and Adam Patrick Murray were joined by regular third chair Brad Chacos to chat about Adam’s time testing Control Resonant, the fall PC game release calendar and the Flydigi Vader 5S PC gamepad. It’s still a streamlined show as Adam packs up his studio for a cross-country move, but of course Alaina came in clutch with those handheld segment titles. PCWorld There was also a good Q&A section where the hosts took questions from the chat and the Discord about everything from favorite games to that query about whether Windows 11 is finally good enough yet or not. It was a fun chat you won’t want to miss! Nerd news of the week I’ve got to make this quick as I’m gearing up for a trip down to L.A. to check out (among other things) that new Lucas Museum of Narrative Art, but even at a glance there’s a smorgasbord of intriguing news in the PC hardware space this week. $14,000 gaming PC features 70 handcrafted titanium cherry blossoms which unfurl as temperatures rise : Sure, 99% of us can’t justify spending $14k on a gaming PC like this no matter how beautiful it is, but we can’t afford to buy a Rothko either. Sometimes art is meant to be appreciated rather than owned, ya know? That’s what I tell myself, at least. Gigabyte admits an oopsie with Gigabyte Control Center software leaving kernel exposed to attackers : If you’ve got a PC running on a Gigabyte motherboard, probably a good idea to update the software sooner rather than later now that some bad folks have compromised the Gigabyte Control Center software. AMD starts the ball rolling for GDDR7 in next-gen GPUs with small code adjustment in its Linux drivers : Sure it might be nothing, but this code change spotted by some eagle-eyed open-source fans suggests AMD is gearing up to catch up to Nvidia by putting GDDR7 memory on its next generation of GPUs. Airbus turned the Steam Deck into a controller for a prototype Mars rover : Uhhh okay, this is just cool. Can you imagine if someone at NASA were piloting a Mars rover using a Steam Deck, and could just Alt + Tab over to Astroneer during downtime? That’s a world we could live in one day. That’s it for your Full Nerd newsletter this week, as I’ve got a plane to catch. Until next week, be sure to bookmark PCWorld and subscribe to the PCWorld YouTube channel !
